extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English poetry; general literate audience interested in literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and critical standards for judging English poetry (particularly comparing Shakespeare and Milton): characterization, passion, imagination, language, versification, originality, and faults. The text surveys what makes dramatic and epic poetry effective and illustrates each point with examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delineation of character (dynamic vs fixed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakespeare's characters are 'liable to be asked all sorts of questions, and are forced to answer for themselves' — they undergo 'continual composition and decomposition' and change with circumstances; Chaucer's characters have a 'fixed essence of character'; Milton 'took only a few simple principles of character, and raised them to the utmost conceivable grandeur.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether characters are portrayed as living, responsive agents who develop under new circumstances (Shakespearean ideal) versus fixed, emblematic types (Chauceran/epic ideal). Consider how much the character's traits are allowed to interact, ferment, and change when placed in new situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of passion (complex, fluctuating vs contemplative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakespeare's passion 'is passion modified by passion... subject to all the fluctuations of caprice and accident' — 'now drunk with hope, now stung to madness' — while Milton 'takes only the imaginative part of passion... which the mind reposes on when all is over.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether emotional life is portrayed as dramatic, immediate, and mutable (producing terror and pity) or as elevated, contemplative, and permanent (producing admiration and delight). Use dramatic scenes (Othello, Lear, Macbeth) as exemplars of fluctuating passion; Milton exemplifies contemplative imaginative passion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic interest vs epic/imaginative interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic poetry affects 'by sympathy, by their nearness to ourselves' and forces us into action; epic affects 'through the medium of the imagination, by magnitude and distance, by their permanence and universality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether a poem's power derives from immediate human vicissitudes and surprise (dramatic) or from grandeur, universality, and imaginative distance (epic). Determine which emotional responses (terror/pity vs admiration/delight) are being sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative range and novelty of combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakespeare 'glances from heaven to earth' and 'brings together images the most alike, but placed at the greatest distance from each other' — remote, rapid combinations that 'startle, and take the fancy prisoner.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the breadth of a poet's associative range and the originality of juxtaposing disparate images. Preference is given to daring, rapid, and surprising combinations that coalesce into striking likenesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision of word-choice (the 'true' word)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Shakespeare 'any other word but the true one, is sure to be wrong' — words 'come winged at his bidding' and 'seem to know their places.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess diction for exactness and inevitability: whether lines feel as if only that specific wording could express the thought or feeling. Test by attempting substitution — if alternatives feel wrong, the choice is felicitous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language register suitability (prose vs elevated diction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakespeare's impassioned language is original and vivid; his 'prose conversation and ordinary business' may be 'technical, and involved in the affectation of the time' and can 'do him offence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the poet appropriately shifts registers between lofty/inspired language and the technical or quotidian; consider whether lower-register passages hinder the work's poetic effect or serve realistic purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versification variety and fitness
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakespeare's versification is 'powerful, sweet, and varied' — from 'measured conversation' to 'lyrical sounds'; Milton's blank verse is similarly musical and adapted to meaning. Milton's lines 'rise or fall, pause or hurry rapidly on, with exquisite art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how well meter, cadence, and rhythm serve the thought and emotion of passages. Look for modulation of sound to sense and for variety appropriate to scene and mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptability of mixed metaphors and elliptical expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakespeare 'abounds in sudden transitions and elliptical expressions' and 'mixed metaphors,' which are 'only abbreviated forms of speech' and often become idioms — they 'give no pain from long custom.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge mixed metaphors not automatically as faults but by effect: do they compress thought into idiom and enrich meaning, or do they jar and obscure? Consider customary usage and whether the expression reads as natural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality vs learned imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton 'has borrowed more than any other writer' and is 'a writer of centos,' yet remains 'perfectly distinct' and 'in originality scarcely inferior to Homer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess balance between learned allusion/borrowing and genuine originality: measure whether learned materials are so assimilated as to produce fresh imaginative force, rather than mere pastiche.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vividness of sensory description
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton 'describes objects... with the vividness of actual observation' across senses (sight, sound, smell), producing 'palpableness and truth' even when learned from books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how concretely and persuasively sensory details are rendered. Strong poetic description should give the impression of direct observation and make images 'tell as pictures.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Force of style
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton's 'force of style' 'stimulates us more in the reading, and less afterwards' — his expression 'makes words tell as pictures' and conveys grandeur and power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the energetic impact of diction and sentence construction: whether style amplifies the subject's grandeur, and whether the prose/poetry exerts compelling imaginative pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical ear and adaptation of sound to meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton possesses 'the same ear for music' and 'power of approximating the varieties of poetical to those of musical rhythm'; his verse is 'moulded into the expression of the sentiment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the poem's sonic qualities: internal music, cadence, repetitions, and how sound patterns echo or enhance semantic content ('linked sweetness long drawn out').

rubrics_metrics.name: Effort, study, and disciplined composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton 'did not write from casual impulse, but after a severe examination of his own strength' and with 'industrious and select reading, steady observation' — he 'always labours, and almost always succeeds.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider evidence of deliberate craft: revision, learned preparation, sustained study. Evaluate whether the work bears marks of careful shaping versus mere spontaneous effusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faults of facility and carelessness
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakespeare's 'natural ease and indifference' and 'very facility of production' sometimes led him to be 'relaxed and careless in critical places' and to make 'blunders in chronology and geography' or excessive puns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify lapses attributable to ease of production: unevenness, occasional lapses in detail, comic excesses (puns), or lack of meticulous arrangement. Distinguish faults that harm poetry from mere period barbarisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and variety of materials chosen
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakespeare 'takes the widest possible range' enabling variety and aptitude of materials, while Milton 'surrounds [subjects] with every possible association of beauty or grandeur.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the poet's selection of subject-matter and associative material: whether breadth enhances the poem's richness and aptness, and whether chosen materials cohere into a unified effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of subject to heroic/demonic portrayal
rubrics_metrics.description: Satan is described as 'the most heroic subject that ever was chosen for a poem' — the poem's interest 'arises from the daring ambition and fierce passions of Satan.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the suitability and boldness of chosen subjects (e.g., heroic anti-heroes) and how effectively the poet sustains interest by dramatizing large ambitions and passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to combine magnitude with human feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic objects affect 'by magnitude and distance' yet Milton combines 'beauty, grandeur, and pathos' so that loss and regret are 'perfect.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the poet's ability to fuse sublime scale with intimate feeling: does grandeur coexist with pathos and human emotion rather than overwhelm it?

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of allusive/learned material as intuitive image-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton's 'learning has the effect of intuition' — he describes things 'of which he could only have read in books, with the vividness of actual observation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether erudition in the poem functions as living imaginative material (intuitive) rather than mere display; check if learned references become pictorial and affective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versification as expressive of meaning (theory/practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton's own theory: 'linked sweetness long drawn out' — versification should pierce the meeting soul and be adapted to sentiment, not reduced to mechanical sing-song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether metrical choices (line-length, pauses, enjambment) are consciously used to enhance meaning and feeling. Beware of mechanical regularity that flattens expression.
